quote_found: There is probably little or no difference between the 'freeze all' strategy and the conventional IVF/ICSI strategy in cumulative live birth rate (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.22; I2 = 0%; 8 RCTs, 4712 women; moderate-quality evidence).
what_is_wrong: Nothing material. I attacked the timing specifically and it holds: Cochrane's Methods define the primary outcome as 'Effectiveness: cumulative live birth rate per randomised woman. That is, the rate of live birth following the transfer of all (fresh or cryopreserved) embryos within the time horizon of the follow-up defined by the authors of the original study' - so the denominator really is the randomised woman and the numerator really is cumulative, not first-transfer. VISUAL READ of Figure 4 (rendered by me): cleavage subgroup Chen 2016 465/746 vs 455/762 OR 1.12 [0.91,1.37], Ferraretti 1999 23/58 vs 26/67 OR 1.04 [0.50,2.13], Vuong 2018 191/391 vs 185/391 OR 1.06 [0.80,1.41], subtotal 1.09 [0.93,1.29] I2=0%; blastocyst subgroup Santos-Ribeiro 2020 65/90 vs 67/94 OR 1.05 [0.55,1.99], Shapiro 2011a 37/70 vs 35/67 OR 1.03 [0.52,2.00], Shapiro 2011b 37/60 vs 39/62 OR 0.95 [0.46,1.97], Wei 2019 627/825 vs 604/825 OR 1.16 [0.93,1.45], Wong 2021 18/102 vs 29/102 OR 0.54 [0.28,1.05], subtotal 1.06 [0.88,1.27] I2=14%; Total 2342 vs 2370, events 1463 vs 1440, diamond 1.08 [0.95,1.22] straddling the null, Chi2=4.83 df=7 P=0.68 I2=0%, Z=1.21 (P=0.23), subgroup difference Chi2=0.07 df=1 P=0.78. Arm counts divide correctly (1463/2342=62.5%, 1440/2370=60.8%) and 2342+2370=4712; subgroup totals 1195+1220=2415 and 1147+1150=2297 both match. Summary of findings 1 reads '579 per 1000 | 589 per 1000 (567 to 627) | OR 1.08 (0.95 to 1.22) | 4712 (8 RCTs) | Moderate', so the claim's +1.0 pp (-1.2 to +4.8) derivation is right. Abstract confirms 'We included 15 studies in the systematic review and eight studies with a total of 4712 women in the meta-analysis' and the sensitivity-analysis internal inconsistency the claim flags is real: the text names five trials (Chen 2016; Santos-Ribeiro 2020; Vuong 2018; Wei 2019; Wong 2021) but says '4 RCTs, 4328 women'. Crossref probe shows CD011184.pub4 returns 404, so pub3 (2021-02-04) is genuinely the latest version. ONE MINOR GLOSS: the claim paraphrases cumulative as 'all transfers arising from one oocyte retrieval'; Cochrane actually says 'within the time horizon of the follow-up defined by the authors of the original study'. These coincide for the constituent trials but are not the same words.

quote_found: Live birth rate calculated after first transfer is added for illustrative purposes as this comparison is often reported in the literature. It possibly shows differences in outcome for a stimulated and an unstimulated uterus, although this does not take into account the number of embryos that were thawed for transfer. This outcome is less relevant for women undergoing treatment since at the same time of first transfer in a freeze-all strategy, they would already have received the second transfer (as long as there was a sufficient number of embryos) in a conventional strategy that includes fresh transfer. Here, one could consider the result of the first embryo transfer in the frozen group against the combined outcomes of the fresh transfer and the first frozen-thawed-transfer in the fresh group. Therefore cumulative live birth rate is the relevant outcome for women.
what_is_wrong: Nothing material. Footnote a is a verbatim match, so the 'illustrative secondary analysis' characterisation is the review's own. VISUAL READ of Analysis 3.1 confirms every cell the claim reports: Aflatoonian 2018 33/121 vs 31/119 OR 1.06 [0.60,1.89]; Aghahosseini 2017 15/36 vs 15/36 OR 1.00 [0.39,2.55]; Chen 2016 368/746 vs 320/762 OR 1.34 [1.10,1.65] (19.0%); Coates 2017 47/61 vs 27/46 OR 2.36 [1.02,5.46]; Ferraretti 1999 23/58 vs 26/67 OR 1.04 [0.50,2.13]; Santos-Ribeiro 2020 42/104 vs 41/105 OR 1.06 [0.61,1.84]; Shapiro 2011a 23/70 vs 10/67 OR 2.79 [1.21,6.44]; Shapiro 2011b 1/62 vs 15/60 OR 0.05 [0.01,0.39] with the arrow running off the left of the plot; Shi 2018 525/1077 vs 542/1080 OR 0.94 [0.80,1.12] (32.8%, largest weight); Stormlund 2020 61/223 vs 66/230 OR 0.94 [0.62,1.41]; Vuong 2018 132/391 vs 123/391 OR 1.11 [0.82,1.50]; Wei 2019 439/825 vs 341/825 OR 1.61 [1.33,1.96] (18.9%); Wong 2021 7/102 vs 22/102 OR 0.27 [0.11,0.66]. Total 3876 vs 3890 (=7766), events 1716 vs 1579, diamond 1.17 [1.06,1.28] lying wholly right of the null; Chi2=46.47 df=12 P<0.00001 I2=74%; Z=3.27 (P=0.001). Crude OR from the totals is 1.163 with 95% CI 1.06-1.27, so the pooled M-H 1.17 (1.06-1.28) is coherent with the arm counts. The five extra trials are named in Table 1 exactly as the claim says. TWO NUANCES, neither a misrepresentation: (a) Cochrane's denominator is 'per randomised woman', not per transfer - the claim's own prose says 'per randomised woman', so the 'per-transfer' tag is a taxonomy label for the first-transfer epoch rather than a denominator statement; (b) Shapiro 2011b's arm totals are swapped between Analysis 1.1 (37/60 vs 39/62) and Analysis 3.1 (1/62 vs 15/60) - that inconsistency is Cochrane's, and the claim transcribes both correctly.

quote_found: No significant difference was found in the live birth rate between the freeze-all and fresh transfer group (61 of 223 (27.4%) and 66 of 230 (28.7%), respectively; risk ratio 0.98, 95% confidence interval 0.87 to 1.10, P=0.83; table 3 ).
what_is_wrong: The headline claim is exactly right (number, population and timing all match), so the verdict is CONFIRMED - but TWO THINGS THE PARENT MUST NOT REPEAT UNCHECKED. (1) The claim's absolute_risk_difference field says the risk difference is 'NOT reported for live birth (the paper reports it for the primary outcome, ongoing pregnancy: -1.8, 95% CI -10.5 to 7.0). COMPUTED BY ME for live birth: 27.4% minus 28.7% = -1.3 percentage points.' That is FALSE. Table 3 reports it, with a confidence interval, in the very row the claim cites: 'Live birth rate/No of randomised women 61/223 (27.4) 66/230 (28.7) -1.3 (-10.1 to 7.4) 0.98 (0.87 to 1.10) 0.83'. The claim presents as its own computation a number the source prints, and omits the CI (-10.1 to 7.4) that the source supplies. (2) SOURCE-LEVEL ANOMALY, not the claim's fault but load-bearing if quoted: the published 'risk ratio 0.98 (0.87 to 1.10)' is not reproducible from 61/223 vs 66/230 - the crude risk ratio is 0.953 with an exact 95% CI of 0.71 to 1.28, so the published interval is far too narrow for a binomial risk ratio on these counts, and it is byte-identical to the ongoing-pregnancy row (62/223 vs 68/230, crude RR 0.939, also published as 0.98, 0.87 to 1.10). Do not present '61/223 vs 66/230; RR 0.98 (0.87-1.10)' as an internally coherent triple. Population verified verbatim: 'Setting Outpatient fertility clinics at eight public hospitals in Denmark, Sweden, and Spain. Participants 460 women aged 18-39 years with regular menstrual cycles starting their first, second, or third treatment cycle of in vitro fertilisation or intracytoplasmic sperm injection.' The claim's careful 'per-woman-randomised' tag is justified: table 3 gives four denominators (randomised women 61/223, started stimulation 61/223, oocyte retrievals 61/221, embryo transfers 56/162) and the claim uses the randomised-woman one, with the 5-woman gap between 61 and 56 explained by 'Five women (2.3%) in the freeze-all group conceived naturally during the pause between oocyte retrieval and blastocyst transfer'. Contamination of the fresh arm verified verbatim (24 women postponed for OHSS risk, six for lack of blastocyst development, seven more for other reasons, 'Only one woman randomised to the freeze-all group had fresh embryo transfer'). Timing is first-transfer-epoch and not cumulative, confirmed by the paper itself: 'Cumulative live birth rates including time to delivery in the cumulative cycles, detailed embryo data, and evaluation of cost effectiveness will be accounted for in separate publications.'

quote_found: Combining all FET from the included oocyte retrievals, the cumulative live birth rate was 42.6% (95/223) in the freeze-all group versus 41.7% (96/230) in the fresh strategy group (risk ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.87-1.19; P = 0.93).

It survives: the title is 'Cumulative live birth rates in a freeze-all or fresh transfer strategy after one ART cycle in ovulatory women', the research question is 'Are cumulative live birth rates similar following a freeze-all strategy compared with a fresh transfer strategy including all subsequent vitrified-warmed cycles from the same oocyte retrieval?', and the follow-up is 'The minimum follow-up time from the start of ovarian stimulation was 2 years' - genuinely cumulative, genuinely per woman randomised, and the same 223/230 denominators as the 2020 index paper. Arithmetic checks: 95/223=42.6%, 96/230=41.7%, crude RR 1.021, RD +0.9 pp. Design descriptor verified: 'The study related to the secondary outcome in a multicentre randomized controlled trial including 460 women allocated in a 1:1 ratio', which corroborates the claim's 'prespecified secondary outcome reported in a separate paper' and dovetails with the 2020 paper's own promise of separate cumulative publications. The notes' extra numbers are also verbatim: median time to first pregnancy 106.0 (80.5-156.5) versus 29.0 (27.0-113.5) days, and deliveries from subsequent FET cycles 15.2% (34/223) versus 12.6% (29/230), P=0.5. ONE FLAG, same as SQ1-C9 and again a source-level property rather than a claim error: the published 95% CI 0.87-1.19 is narrower than the exact binomial interval for these counts (0.82 to 1.27), so this group's reported risk-ratio intervals should not be re-derived from the cell counts.

I also independently verified the protocol record via Europe PMC REST for PMID 35851030.
quote_found: IPD from 12 trials involving 8,246 randomised participants were obtained. All 12 studies reported live births after the first transfer. IPD meta-analysis showed no evidence that a freeze-all embryo transfer strategy differed from a fresh embryo transfer on live birth rate following the first transfer (43.9% vs 41.1%, adjusted risk ratio (RR) 1.04, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.92 to 1.18, I 2 50%).
what_is_wrong: The claim's central assertion is refuted. It states 'As of this search there is NO published individual-participant-data meta-analysis of freeze-all versus fresh transfer: the INFORM IPD meta-analysis exists only as a protocol'. INFORM results are published, in three places, and the most SQ1-relevant one reports precisely the outcome this sub-question is about. (1) Fertility and Sterility, October 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.fertnstert.2024.07.251, 'WHO BENEFITS MOST FROM A FREEZE-ALL EMBRYO TRANSFER STRATEGY? AN INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPANT DATA META-ANALYSIS OF RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIALS (INFORM)', Wang R, Au LS, Wei D, ... Legro RS, Wang Z, Sun Y, Wu K, Vuong LN et al: 'The primary outcome was live birth following the first transfer', results as quoted above, and 'CONCLUSIONS The freeze-all and fresh embryo transfer strategies did not differ significantly in overall live birth rate following the first transfer, although a freeze-only strategy benefitted patients with elevated progesterone levels on trigger day.' (2) Human Reproduction 40(Supplement_1), June 2025, DOI 10.1093/humrep/deaf097.1086, 'P-782 Obstetric and Neonatal Outcomes following Freeze-all vs Fresh Embryo Transfer Strategies: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomised Trials (INFORM)' (Au N, Wang R, Wei D, Vuong LN, Pinborg AB et al), 12 RCTs, 8222 participants, hypertensive disorders 2.9% vs 1.8% aRR 1.66, LGA 17.8% vs 13.1% aRR 1.38, SGA 5.7% vs 8.1% aRR 0.71, and it states in terms 'Our earlier work on this IPD-MA found no significant live birth rate differences between the two groups'. (3) A full results manuscript is posted as a 2026 preprint, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7001926, 'Frozen Versus Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF - An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials (INFORM)', with the full INFORM author list and the same PROSPERO registration CRD42021296566: search 'up until 24 September 2025', 'Among 16 eligible trials, IPD from 13 trials involving 9060 randomised participants (96% of eligible participants) were obtained', primary outcome 'live birth following the first embryo transfer', result 'no evidence that a freeze-all embryo transfer strategy differed from a fresh embryo transfer on live birth rate following the first transfer (adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 1.00, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.17, moderate-certainty evidence)', plus OHSS aRR 0.28 (0.18 to 0.43, high certainty) and major congenital anomaly aRR 0.73 (0.63 to 0.85), and the interpretation 'In unselected IVF population, the freeze-all and fresh embryo transfer strategies are comparable in terms of live birth rate following the first transfer'. WHY THE CLAIM MISSED IT: its stated search used PubMed and OpenAlex only, and neither indexes ASRM/ESHRE abstracts published in Fertility and Sterility or Human Reproduction supplements, nor SSRN preprints; the Europe PMC citation list for the protocol has just one entry. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR SQ1, beyond the bibliographic point: the claim's own note argues 'the IPD will therefore not by itself resolve the cumulative question'. That framing now needs revising, because the IPD result on the per-first-transfer outcome is NULL (aRR 1.00, 0.86-1.17 in the full analysis; 1.04, 0.92-1.18 in the earlier 12-trial version) and therefore directly contradicts Cochrane's pooled per-first-transfer OR 1.17 (1.06-1.28) with I2=74% - the IPD analysis, adjusted for age and BMI and using 96% of eligible participants, brings the per-transfer estimate into line with the cumulative null rather than leaving the two timings in conflict. WHAT SURVIVES: the protocol itself is real and correctly described - I verified via Europe PMC that BMJ Open 2022 PMID 35851030 states 'The primary outcome will be live birth resulting from the first embryo transfer', that PROSPERO registration is CRD42021296566, and that 'The search was performed on 23 September 2020 and will be updated'. The quote the claim attributes to the protocol is verbatim.
